heading: Abstract
text:
\nNeural networks transform data through learned representations whose
geometry affects separation, contraction, and generalization. Recent work
studies this geometry using discrete curvature on neighborhood graphs,
suggesting Ricci-flow-like behavior across layers. We develop a smooth
operator-theoretic alternative for feedforward representation snapshots.
Each feature cloud induces a Gaussian-kernel diffusion Markov operator, and
transport, spectral, label-boundary, and local-scale observables are derived
from this single object via Bakry–Émery Γ\Gamma-calculus. In a
balanced Gaussian class-conditional snapshot model with shared covariance,
the population operator has closed-form class affinities, leakage, and
coarse spectra, all controlled by pairwise regularized Mahalanobis separations
cε(a,b)c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}. We also prove that the resulting operator observables vary smoothly under
feature perturbations, while hard neighborhood-graph diagnostics can change
discontinuously. Synthetic experiments validate the closed-form Gaussian bridge, while
learned MNIST experiments show that the same operator observables
track training, width, and perturbation stability. Together, these results
give a stable operator-geometric framework for analyzing feedforward
representation geometry.

heading: 1 Introduction
text:
\n
\nNeural networks reshape data through their learned representations. If
Φℓ:ℝd0→ℝdℓ\Phi_{\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}} denotes the map from
input space to layer ℓ\ell, then the feature cloud


\n

Zℓ={ziℓ}i=1n,ziℓ=Φℓ​(xi),Z^{\ell}=\{z_{i}^{\ell}\}_{i=1}^{n},\qquad z_{i}^{\ell}=\Phi_{\ell}(x_{i}),


\nevolves with both depth and training. These evolving snapshots often become
more separable, lower-dimensional, and aligned with label structure
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Understanding their
geometry is therefore a natural route toward understanding representation
learning.

\n
\nA recent line of work studies this geometry by constructing neighborhood
graphs on feature clouds and measuring discrete geometric quantities such as
graph curvature, curvature gaps, and Ricci-flow-inspired evolution
coefficients [7, 8]. This viewpoint is
appealing because it connects class separation with community formation and
local representation changes with geometric flows. However, hard graph
constructions introduce a basic instability. Small perturbations of the
feature cloud can rewire a kk-nearest-neighbor graph, and the resulting
geometry can depend strongly on graph parameters such as neighborhood size,
radius, symmetrization, and curvature discretization
[9, 10, 11, 12, 13].

\n
\nWe take an operator-first view. Instead of first constructing a hard graph,
we associate each representation snapshot with a smooth diffusion Markov
operator, following the kernel-normalization viewpoint of diffusion maps [14, 15]. For a bandwidth ε>0\varepsilon>0, define


\n

Wi​jℓ=exp⁡(−‖ziℓ−zjℓ‖24​ε),Pℓ=(Dℓ)−1​Wℓ,Lℓ=Pℓ−Iε.W_{ij}^{\ell}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|z_{i}^{\ell}-z_{j}^{\ell}\|^{2}}{4\varepsilon}\right),\qquad P^{\ell}=(D^{\ell})^{-1}W^{\ell},\qquad L^{\ell}=\frac{P^{\ell}-I}{\varepsilon}.


\nThe associated carré du champ operator is


\n

Γℓ​(f,h)​(i)=12​ε​∑jPi​jℓ​(fj−fi)​(hj−hi).\Gamma^{\ell}(f,h)(i)=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon} um_{j}P_{ij}^{\ell}(f_{j}-f_{i})(h_{j}-h_{i}).


\nFrom this single operator we derive class-level transport, coarse spectra,
label-boundary energies, soft diffusion radii, and local metric surrogates.
Thus the primitive object is not a graph curvature score, but a Markov
operator from which several geometric observables are derived
[16, 17, 18, 19].

\n
\nThe main theoretical object is a solvable Gaussian snapshot model. At a
fixed layer and training time, suppose


\n

\nwith balanced classes and shared covariance. We show that the coarse
operator geometry is controlled by


\n

cε(a,b)=14​(μa−μb)⊤​(ε​I+Σ)−1​(μa−μb).c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}=\tfrac{1}{4}(\mu_{a}-\mu_{b})^{\top}(\varepsilon I+\Sigma)^{-1}(\mu_{a}-\mu_{b}).


\nThese separations determine normalized affinities, cross-class leakage, and
the spectrum of the induced coarse class-transition operator. In the
homogeneous case, the resulting formulas become closed-form and monotone.
Increasing regularized class separation decreases leakage and changes the
coarse spectral gap in an explicit way.

\n
\nWe also prove a stability result. For fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 and bounded
feature clouds, the map Z↦Pε​(Z)Z\mapsto P_{\varepsilon}(Z) is locally Lipschitz.
Consequently, the induced leakage, boundary energy, coarse transition, and
soft local-scale observables vary continuously under feature perturbations.
By contrast, hard kk-nearest-neighbor adjacency-dependent quantities are
discontinuous at configurations where neighbor orderings change. This gives
a formal explanation for the stability advantage of the operator
construction [20, 21].

heading: Contributions.
text:
\n
\nWe make four contributions. First, we formalize feedforward representation
snapshots as diffusion Markov operators and derive transport, spectral,
label-boundary, and local-scale observables from this single object. Second,
under a balanced shared-covariance Gaussian snapshot model, we prove a
closed-form bridge showing that coarse operator geometry is governed by the
regularized Mahalanobis separations cε(a,b)c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}, yielding
explicit formulas for affinities, leakage, and class spectra. Third, we
prove that the diffusion operator and its induced observables are locally
Lipschitz under feature perturbations, while hard kk-nearest-neighbor
graph observables can be discontinuous. Finally, synthetic Gaussian experiments validate the closed-form bridge,
while learned ten-class MNIST experiments show that the operator
observables give stable, interpretable measurements across training, width,
and perturbations.

heading: 2 Related work
text:
\n
\nLearned representations have been studied through intrinsic dimension,
separability, topology, similarity, and neural collapse
[1, 2, 3, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4, 26, 5].
Recent graph-geometric work instead constructs neighborhood graphs on
features and measures discrete curvature or Ricci-flow-inspired quantities
[9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 7, 8]. Our approach differs by taking a
diffusion Markov operator as the primitive object, avoiding hard adjacency
choices and yielding KK-class transport, spectral, boundary, and
local-scale observables from one operator. The construction is closest in
language to diffusion maps and diffusion geometry
[14, 15, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33] and to Bakry–Émery
Γ\Gamma-calculus for Markov operators
[16, 17, 18, 19].

\nThis behavior contrasts with hard neighborhood graphs. Let Ak​(Z)A_{k}(Z) be
the adjacency matrix of a kk-nearest-neighbor graph built from ZZ,
with any fixed tie-breaking rule.

\n

heading: Proposition 3 (Discontinuity of hard kk-NN adjacency).
text:
\n
\nFor 1≤k<n−11\leq k<n-1, the map Z↦Ak​(Z)Z\mapsto A_{k}(Z) is discontinuous at any
feature cloud where, for some point ziz_{i}, the kk-th and (k+1)(k+1)-st
nearest-neighbor distances are equal. Consequently, any graph observable
that depends nontrivially on this adjacency can change discontinuously
under arbitrarily small feature perturbations.


\n

heading: Proof.
text:
\n
\nAt such a tie, arbitrarily small perturbations can reverse the order of the
two neighbors. Along one perturbation, one neighbor is included in the
kk-nearest-neighbor set of ii; along another, the other is included.
Thus an adjacency entry changes by one under perturbations of arbitrarily
small norm, and any observable that distinguishes these adjacency patterns
inherits the discontinuity.
∎


\n
\nTogether, Theorem 2 and
Proposition 3 give a stability-discontinuity
dichotomy. Under the same feature perturbation, the diffusion operator
changes by O⁡(‖Z−Z~‖∞)O(\|Z-\widetilde{Z}\|_{\infty}), while hard kk-NN adjacency
can change by Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1). This is the formal content of the stability
advantage tested empirically in Section 6.

heading: 6 Empirical evaluation
text:
\n
\nWe evaluate the operator framework along three axes. First, we test whether
the Gaussian bridge predicts empirical operator observables in the
controlled setting where its assumptions hold. Second, we measure how the
operator observables evolve across training and width in learned
feedforward representations. Third, we test whether operator observables
are more stable than hard-neighborhood graph observables under small
perturbations.

\n
\nUnless otherwise stated, all learned-representation experiments use a
two-hidden-layer ReLU MLP trained on ten-class MNIST. We report the
mean pairwise separation c¯ε\bar{c}_{\varepsilon}, cross-class leakage, the
coarse mixing gap 1−λ2​(P^(K))1-\lambda_{2}(\widehat{P}^{(K)}), and the root-mean-square
soft diffusion radius. For the perturbation experiment we also report the
one-hot label-boundary energy E⁡[Γ⁡(g,g)]E[\Gamma(g,g)].

\n
\nFor empirical coarse-transition calculations, we remove point self-loops
from the diffusion operator and renormalize rows before aggregating by
class. This avoids a finite-sample artifact from the diagonal kernel
entries Wi​i=1W_{ii}=1. The population formulas in
Section 4 describe the class-level large-sample
limit, where individual point self-loops vanish. Implementation details,
including bandwidth selection, subset sizes, and hard-graph baselines, are
given in Appendix C.

\n
\nFor consistency with Proposition 1, the leakage
we report from the empirical class-transition matrix is the stationary
leakage of the coarse chain. The raw node-average leakage defined in
Section 3 is a related but distinct finite-sample
observable.

heading: 6.1 Synthetic validation of the Gaussian bridge
text:
\n
\nWe first test the Gaussian bridge in the setting where its assumptions
hold. We sample balanced K=4K=4 Gaussian class-conditionals in dimension
d=16d=16 with shared covariance, vary both class separation and bandwidth
ε\varepsilon, and compare empirical operator quantities with the
population formulas of Section 4.


Figure 1: Gaussian bridge validation.
Theory versus empirical measurements for balanced Gaussian
class-conditionals. Left: mean pairwise separation
c¯ε\bar{c}_{\varepsilon}. Middle: cross-class leakage. Right: coarse
mixing gap 1−λ21-\lambda_{2}. The dashed line is the identity. The bridge
closely predicts the finite-sample operator observables across
separations and bandwidths.

\n
\nFigure 1 confirms the closed-form population bridge in
the regime it is designed to describe. The agreement supports
{cε(a,b)}\{c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}\} as the reduced state variable for coarse
operator geometry under the Gaussian snapshot model.

heading: 6.2 Training dynamics
text:
\n
\nWe next track the operator observables over training. To isolate geometric
change from bandwidth drift, each hidden layer uses a fixed bandwidth chosen
from its initialization snapshot. This convention measures the learned
representation at a fixed diffusion scale. In later epochs, especially in
deeper layers, sharp changes in leakage or gap indicate that feature
separation has expanded beyond the initial kernel scale. We also inspect
the full pairwise separation matrix
{cε(a,b)}\{c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}\} in the deepest layer.


\n
\n\n\n
Figure 2: Training-time evolution of operator geometry.
Top: across hidden layers, training increases mean separation
c¯ε\bar{c}_{\varepsilon}, reduces cross-class leakage, decreases the
coarse mixing gap, and contracts the soft diffusion radius. Bandwidths
are fixed from initialization, so late sharp drops reflect features
moving beyond the initial diffusion scale. Bottom: the full
separation matrix in the deepest hidden layer at selected epochs.
Training changes the full class-pair geometry, not only a single scalar
separation scale.

\n
\nThe trends in Figure 2 show that the operator
observables track the emergence of class structure during training. As
regularized class separation increases, cross-class diffusion weakens and
the class-level chain becomes more persistent. The heatmaps show that this
evolution is not captured by a single global statistic. Different class
pairs separate at different rates, so the full matrix
{cε(a,b)}\{c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}\} contains information lost by its mean alone.

heading: 6.3 Width dependence
text:
\n
\nTo study model scale, we fix depth and vary hidden width. For this
experiment, each feature cloud is centered and divided by its RMS feature
norm before constructing the operator. All widths are then evaluated using
a common reference bandwidth ε⋆\varepsilon^{ tar}, chosen from a baseline
model after the same normalization. This isolates relative representation
geometry from global feature-scale changes.


Figure 3: Width dependence of scale-normalized operator observables.
Each feature cloud is centered and divided by its RMS feature norm before
operator construction, and all widths use a common reference bandwidth.
Increasing width raises mean class separation c¯ε\bar{c}_{\varepsilon} and
the weakest pairwise separation
cmin=mina≠b⁡cε(a,b)c_{\min}=\min_{a\neq b}c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}, while cross-class leakage
decreases modestly and the coarse mixing gap changes weakly. Shaded bands
indicate Student-tt 95%95\% confidence intervals across ten seeds.

\n
\nFigure 3 shows that width affects scale-normalized
representation geometry selectively. Wider models achieve larger mean
regularized class separation c¯ε\bar{c}_{\varepsilon}, and the weakest
class-pair separation cminc_{\min} also increases substantially.
Cross-class leakage decreases modestly, while the coarse mixing gap
changes only weakly. Thus, increasing width primarily improves class-pair
separation at a fixed normalized diffusion scale.

heading: 6.4 Stability versus hard neighborhood graphs
text:
\n
\nFinally, we test the main methodological motivation for replacing hard
graphs with a diffusion operator. We perturb a fixed learned feature cloud
with small additive Gaussian noise, recompute operator observables and hard
mutual kk-NN graph observables, and measure variability across
perturbations.


Figure 4: Operator observables are more stable than hard-graph
observables.
A learned feature cloud is repeatedly perturbed with small Gaussian
noise. Top: absolute standard deviation across perturbations. Bottom:
relative standard deviation. Error bars show one standard deviation
across perturbations. Operator leakage, E⁡[Γ⁡(g,g)]E[\Gamma(g,g)], and soft
radius vary substantially less than their hard kk-NN graph
counterparts.

\n
\nFigure 4 gives the clearest empirical advantage of the
operator-first construction. Hard-neighborhood observables inherit
adjacency-level discontinuities and can change abruptly when perturbations
rewire edges. In contrast, the diffusion operator varies smoothly with the
feature cloud, yielding substantially more stable transport, boundary, and
local-scale diagnostics.

heading: 7 Discussion
text:
\n
\nThis paper develops an operator geometry for feedforward representation
snapshots. A feature cloud ZZ is represented by a diffusion Markov
operator Pε​(Z)P_{\varepsilon}(Z), from which transport, spectra,
label-boundary energy, local scale, and Γ\Gamma-geometry are all
derived. The Gaussian bridge gives one solvable instance of this
abstraction. Under a balanced shared-covariance Gaussian snapshot model,
the coarse operator geometry is controlled by


\n

cε(a,b)=14​(μa−μb)⊤​(ε​I+Σ)−1​(μa−μb),c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}=\frac{1}{4}(\mu_{a}-\mu_{b})^{\top}(\varepsilon I+\Sigma)^{-1}(\mu_{a}-\mu_{b}),


\nso the operator measures class separation at diffusion scale
ε\varepsilon through a covariance-regularized metric. Coarse quantities
such as affinities, leakage, and class spectra reduce to the separation
matrix {cε(a,b)}\{c_{\varepsilon}^{(a,b)}\}, while local quantities such as
Γ\Gamma-Gram matrices and soft radii retain directional covariance
information. The stability theorem adds a second structural point. At
fixed bandwidth, the Gaussian-kernel operator is a smooth function of
ZZ and its observables inherit this stability, while hard neighborhood
graphs instead pass through a discontinuous adjacency-selection step.

\n
\nThe framework is built for feedforward snapshots, where a layer is
treated as a map from one feature cloud to the next. This viewpoint is
complementary to kernel-limit, neural tangent kernel, and
signal-propagation analyses
[34, 35, 36, 37], since our object is
the diffusion operator induced by a finite learned feature cloud. Other
architectures induce different operator objects. Recurrent models suggest
finite-lag, irreversible transport operators, and Transformers suggest
operator geometries built from attention laws, token measures, or
conditional Markov kernels rather than Euclidean clouds
[38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44]. A further direction within
feedforward snapshots is to study pointwise leakage scores and their
upper tails, which may separate collapsed class cores from boundary mass
in learned representations. The contribution here is an analyzable
alternative to the hard-graph diagnostics targeted by Ricci-flow-inspired
feature geometry. Representation geometry becomes the study of stable
diffusion operators whose class-level behavior can be solved in
population models and measured directly in learned networks.

heading: A.6 Mean-field interpretation
text:
\n
\nThe formulas above are population and mean-field statements. The affinity
identity in Theorem 1 is an exact population
expectation. The coarse chain is the class-level Markov chain obtained by
row-normalizing those population affinities. Finite empirical operators
fluctuate around this limit because they depend on the sampled feature
cloud, finite class counts, and the self-loop entries Wi​i=1W_{ii}=1.

\n
\nFor large balanced samples, the contribution of a single self-loop to a row
sum is O⁡(1)O(1), while the total off-diagonal affinity mass is typically
O⁡(n)O(n). Thus the block-constant population chain provides the natural
large-sample approximation to the empirical class transition matrix.

heading: B.5 Discontinuity of hard neighborhood graphs
text:
\n
\nWe now prove Proposition 3. Let
Ak​(Z)A_{k}(Z) denote the adjacency matrix of a directed kk-nearest-neighbor
graph, with an arbitrary but fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule. The
same argument applies to symmetrized kk-nearest-neighbor graphs whenever
the changed directed edge affects the symmetrized adjacency.

\n
\nFix 1≤k<n−11\leq k<n-1. Suppose there exists a point ziz_{i} for which the
kk-th and (k+1)(k+1)-st nearest-neighbor distances are equal. That is,
there are two distinct candidate neighbors zpz_{p} and zqz_{q} such that


\n

‖zi−zp‖=‖zi−zq‖=r,\|z_{i}-z_{p}\|=\|z_{i}-z_{q}\|=r,


\nand exactly k−1k-1 other points are strictly closer to ziz_{i}.

\n
\nAssume that the tie-breaking rule selects pp rather than qq, so that


\n

Ak​(Z)i​p=1,Ak​(Z)i​q=0.A_{k}(Z)_{ip}=1,\qquad A_{k}(Z)_{iq}=0.


\nFor any η>0\eta>0, we can perturb zpz_{p} and zqz_{q} by less than
η\eta so that zqz_{q} becomes slightly closer to ziz_{i} than zpz_{p},
while all other neighbor orderings remain unchanged. Denote the perturbed
cloud by Z(η)Z^{(\eta)}. Then


\n

‖Z(η)−Z‖∞<η,\|Z^{(\eta)}-Z\|_{\infty}<\eta,


\nbut


\n

Ak​(Z(η))i​p=0,Ak​(Z(η))i​q=1.A_{k}(Z^{(\eta)})_{ip}=0,\qquad A_{k}(Z^{(\eta)})_{iq}=1.


\nThus an adjacency entry changes by one under an arbitrarily small
perturbation. Hence Z↦Ak​(Z)Z\mapsto A_{k}(Z) is discontinuous at ZZ.

\n
\nIf a graph observable M​(Ak​(Z))M(A_{k}(Z)) takes different values on these two
adjacency patterns, then


\n

M⁡(Ak​(Z(η)))↛M⁡(Ak​(Z))M(A_{k}(Z^{(\eta)}))\not\to M(A_{k}(Z))


\nas η→0\eta\to 0. Thus any adjacency-dependent observable that nontrivially
distinguishes the two graphs is also discontinuous at such a
neighbor-swap configuration.

heading: Appendix C Implementation Details
text:
\n
\nThis appendix summarizes the computational choices used in the reported
experiments.

heading: Reported runs.
text:
\n
\nThe unified experiment script supports both reduced multiclass and larger
multiclass runs. By default, the script is configured for reduced
multiclass experiments, while the learned-representation figures reported
in the paper are generated within the ten-class MNIST setting.

\n
\nThese reported learned-representation figures include training dynamics,
pairwise separation heatmaps, width sweeps, and stability experiments. The
synthetic bridge validation remains a K=4K=4 shared-covariance Gaussian
mixture experiment.

heading: Operator construction.
text:
\n
\nGiven a feature snapshot


\n

Z={zi}i=1n⊂ℝd,Z=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} ubset\mathbb{R}^{d},


\nwe form the Gaussian affinity matrix


\n

Wi​j=exp⁡(−‖zi−zj‖24​ε),W_{ij}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}}{4\varepsilon}\right),


\nthe degree vector


\n

Di=∑j=1nWi​j,D_{i}= um_{j=1}^{n}W_{ij},


\nand the row-stochastic diffusion operator


\n

Pi​j=Wi​jDi.P_{ij}=\frac{W_{ij}}{D_{i}}.


\nWhen needed for spectral calculations, we also form the symmetric operator


\n

H=D−1/2WD−1/2.H=D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}.


\nUnless otherwise stated, we use the raw-kernel construction, corresponding
to α=0\alpha=0 in the diffusion-maps normalization family.

\n

εmed=14​mediani<j​‖zi−zj‖2.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{med}}=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{median}_{i<j}\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}.


\nWhen the snapshot contains more than 20002000 points, this median is
estimated from a random subset of at most 20002000 points. Depending on the
experiment, we either fix ε\varepsilon from an initialization snapshot or
use a single reference bandwidth across a sweep.

text:
\n
\nAll reported operator experiments are KK-class experiments. Let
μ^a\hat{\mu}_{a} denote the empirical mean of class aa, and let

text:
\n
\nTo define class-level transport observables, we construct a coarse

\n

matrix

text:

\nThe width sweep fixes depth and varies only the hidden width. The reported
configuration uses widths


\n

{16,32,64,128,256,512,1024},\{16,32,64,128,256,512,1024\},


\n15 training epochs, Adam with learning rate 10−310^{-3}, and seeds

{0,1,…,9}.\{0,1,\dots,9\}.

heading: Stability experiment.
text:
\n
\nFor the stability experiment, we train the same (128,128)(128,128) MLP for
15 epochs and extract features from each hidden layer on the balanced
evaluation subset. For each layer, we fix the operator bandwidth using the
unperturbed snapshot and compute baseline operator and graph metrics.

\n
\nThe reported main-text figure uses additive Gaussian perturbations of the
feature cloud,


\n

z~i=zi+σ​ξi,ξi∼𝒩⁡(0,I),\widetilde{z}_{i}=z_{i}+ igma\xi_{i},\qquad\xi_{i} im\mathcal{N}(0,I),


\nwith σ=10−3 igma=10^{-3}. For each seed and each hidden layer, we generate

radius.

\n
\nFor the hard-graph baseline, hard-graph leakage is the average fraction of
mutual neighbors with a different label, and the hard-graph local radius is
the root mean squared edge length averaged over mutual neighbors. The
label-disagreement score serves as the hard-graph analogue of the operator
boundary energy, being a normalized graph quantity and isn’t scaled by
1/ε1/\varepsilon, so the relative standard deviation is the
scale-comparable stability statistic. Nodes with zero mutual degree
contribute zero to all node-averaged hard-graph quantities.
